sentences.text:
. The instant proceedings have originated out of a complaint filed by Mr. Hundi Lal against Mr.
Surender Kumar @ Yash Kumar Chhoker for the offense under Section 138, Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as "NI Act").
2.

The complainant claims that on 07.03.2023, he and his daughter met the accused and his partner,
Mr. Abhinav Singh, at Patiala House Courts for legal advice.
During this period, the complainant advanced a total sum of Rs. 8,23,000/- to the accused and his partner through cash, RTGS, net banking, and UPI.
Alleging that the accused misled him, the complainant demanded a refund of the amount on 09.06.2023.
On 13.06.2023, during a meeting at the accused's chamber, the accused agreed to return Rs. 4 lakhs immediately and the remaining Rs. 4.23 lakhs later.
Accordingly, the accused issued two cheques, no. 961296 and 961297, each for Rs. 2 lakhs, dated 15.07.2023, and also handed over a written promissory note acknowledging his liability.
3. On 20.07.2023, both cheques were dishonored due to insufficient funds.
The complainant sent an intimation letter before depositing the cheques and later issued a legal notice on 03.08.2023, which was duly served on the accused on 07.08.2023.
Despite this, the accused failed to make the payment within the statutory period of 15 days.
Consequently, the complainant filed the present complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881.

The complainant (CW-1) was cross-examined on 30.05.2024.
7.

The complainant stated that the first payment was made by his daughter through his account--Rs.
40,000/- to Mr. Rohit and Rs. 10,000/- to Mr. Abhinav.
He claimed that the remaining amount came from his savings and was paid in cash in the presence of his daughter, Mr. Saurav Kumar, and Mr. Abhinav.
He denied the suggestion that no payment was made to the accused and stated that online payments to Mr. Abhinav and Mr. Rohit were made at the accused's request.
He confirmed that the promissory note was executed at the time of cheque issuance, with Mr. Subhash Lohia as a witness.
He acknowledged that the cheques were given as security but had not seen their backside.
He reiterated that he had paid a total of Rs. 8.23 lakhs to Mr. Abhinav, Mr. Rohit, and the accused.
8. CW-2, Ms. Medha Kaushwaha (complainant's daughter), was examined on 06.08.2024.

She stated that she did not transfer money directly to the accused's account but handed over Rs. 5.23 Hundi Lal vs Surender Kumar @Yash Kumar Chhoker on 7 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/131159148/
2 lakhs in cash at Mr. Abhinav Singh's request.

sentences.text: With this, the complainant's evidence was closed.
9. On 22.08.2024, the accused was examined under Section 313 Cr.P.C., where all incriminating evidence was put to him.
He reiterated that the cheques were given as security in connection with a dispute under Section 420 IPC, which he helped settle.
He denied any liability for the cheque amount but admitted signing the promissory note.
He also acknowledged receiving the legal demand notice and responding to it.
Given the opportunity to present defence evidence, the accused declined on 06.11.2024, leading to the closure of DE and the commencement of final arguments.
10. Learned counsel for the complainant argued that since the accused has admitted his signatures on the cheques, the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act is attracted.

Additionally,
the accused has also admitted his signature on the promissory note, further affirming his liability.
The burden of proof lies on the accused to rebut the presumption, but he has failed to produce any evidence in support of his defense.
As the accused has not discharged his burden, the presumption remains unrebutted, and he is liable to be convicted under Section 138 of the NI Act.
11. Learned counsel for the accused argued that the complainant has failed to establish a clear and legally enforceable liability against the accused.

The cross-examination of the complainant and his witnesses reveals that the alleged payments SIDDHANT KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2025.02.07 15:16:21 +0530 Hundi Lal Vs. Surender Kumar @ Yash Kumar Chhoker Page No.5 of 9 were made to third parties, not directly to the accused.

sentences.text: Since no funds were transferred to the accused, no legally enforceable debt or liability arises against him.
Furthermore, the complainant failed to examine the witness to the promissory note, weakening its evidentiary value.

The inconsistencies in the complainant's case,
coupled with the absence of direct financial transactions with the accused, create serious doubts about the alleged liability.
Therefore, the accused should be acquitted.

12. Under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, a statutory presumption exists in favor of the holder of the cheque that it was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or Hundi Lal vs Surender Kumar @Yash Kumar Chhoker on 7 February, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/131159148/
3 liability.

sentences.text: In the present case, the accused has admitted the issuance and signatures on the cheques in question.

As per the judgment in Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa, 2019 SCC OnLine SC 491, once the execution of the cheque is admitted, a presumption under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act is raised that the cheque was issued towards a legally enforceable debt or liability.

entities.text: Basalingappa v. Mudibasappa, 2019 SCC OnLine SC 491
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, this presumption is rebuttable, and the burden lies on the accused to disprove it on the touchstone of a preponderance of probabilities.
13. Further, as held in Rajesh Jain v. Ajay Singh, SLP (Crl.) No. 12802 of 2022, if the accused fails to rebut the presumption, the court can proceed with conviction.

entities.text: Rajesh Jain v. Ajay Singh, SLP (Crl.) No. 12802 of 2022
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: However, if the presumption is successfully rebutted, the burden shifts back to the complainant, who must then establish the existence of a legally enforceable debt beyond a reasonable doubt.

sentences.text: The defense taken by the accused is that no legally enforceable debt or liability exists.
He claims that the payments were not made directly to him but to other persons, as reflected in the cross-examination of CW-1 and CW-2.

He further asserts in his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
that he acted as a mediator between the complainant and his associates in a dispute under Section 420 IPC and that the cheques were issued as security in connection with that settlement.
15. A critical analysis of the evidence on record reveals that the accused has failed to substantiate his defense.
Although he asserts that he was merely a mediator, he has not produced any witness or documentary evidence to support this claim.
The accused has admitted his signatures on the promissory note, which explicitly records a liability of Rs. 4 lakhs and mentions the cheque numbers in question.
Documentary evidence, particularly a written promissory note, holds higher evidentiary value than mere oral claims, and its contents affirm the existence of liability.
The promissory note clearly stipulates that the payment of Rs. 4 lakhs was to be made by 15.07.2023 or earlier, and upon such payment, the cheques were to be returned.
However, no evidence has been presented by the accused to establish that any such payment was ever made.
16. The cheques were presented for encashment on 20.07.2023 and dishonored due to insufficient funds.

The complainant had acted in accordance with the terms of the promissory note, and in SIDDHANT KUMAR KUMAR Date:

sentences.text: the absence of any evidence from the accused proving repayment, the liability remained intact.
The defense that the cheques were given merely as security is not tenable, as the promissory note itself records a specific monetary obligation.
A security cheque, when linked to an underlying liability that remains unpaid, is legally enforceable.
17. Given that the accused has not led any defense evidence or examined any witness to rebut the presumption of liability, the presumption under Section 139 NI Act remains unrebutted.
In such a scenario, as laid down in Rajesh Jain v. Ajay Singh, the court can proceed with conviction if all other procedural requirements under Section 138 NI Act are fulfilled.
18. In the present case, all other procedural requirements under Section 138 NI Act have been duly complied with:
The cheques were issued for a legally enforceable debt by the accused and presented within their validity period.
The cheques were dishonored due to insufficient funds.

The complainant issued a statutory legal notice on 03.08.2023,
which was duly served upon the accused on 07.08.2023.
Despite service of notice, the accused failed to make the payment within the statutory 15-day period.
The complaint was filed within the limitation period.

19. In light of the above discussion, the accused has failed to Digitally signed by SIDDHANT SIDDHANT KUMAR KUMAR Date:
2025.02.07 15:16:34 CT Case No. 7585/2023 +0530 Hundi Lal Vs. Surender Kumar @ Yash Kumar Chhoker Page No.8 of 9 rebut the presumption of a legally enforceable debt or liability, and the complainant has successfully proved his case.

The necessary ingredients for an offense under Section 138 NI Act stand satisfied,
warranting the conviction of the accused.
20. Therefore, the court is presented with a compelling basis to proceed with conviction, holding the accused guilty for the offense under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
Accused Surender Kumar, is hereby convicted for the offense punishable u/s 138 NI Act qua the cheque in the present case.
